scenes.heading: Caching
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Caching and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: Why cache
items: Reuse a computed DataFrame across actions
Avoid recomputing the whole DAG each time
scenes.narration: Caching tells Spark to keep a computed DataFrame around so later actions reuse it instead of recomputing the entire lineage. Because Spark is lazy, an uncached DataFrame is rebuilt from scratch every time you act on it. The cache method is simply a shortcut for persisting with the default memory-and-disk storage level.

scenes.heading: Caching lifecycle
scenes.narration: Calling cache only marks a DataFrame for caching; nothing is stored until the first action materializes it. On that first pass Spark computes the data and writes the blocks into executor memory. Subsequent actions then read from those cached blocks, skipping the upstream work. When you no longer need it, calling unpersist releases the memory.

scenes.code:
base = spark.read.parquet("/data/txns").filter("amount > 0")
base.cache()
base.count()          # materializes the cache
top = base.groupBy("user").sum("amount")   # reuses cache
cnt = base.groupBy("region").count()       # reuses cache
base.unpersist()
scenes.heading: Cache once, reuse many times
scenes.narration: Here the filtered base is cached and then a count forces it to materialize. The two aggregations that follow both read from the cached data rather than re-reading and re-filtering the source. Without caching, each aggregation would replay the entire read-and-filter pipeline. Finally unpersist frees the blocks once the reuse is done.

scenes.text: Only cache when a DataFrame is reused; caching once-used data just wastes memory.
scenes.narration: Caching is a win when a dataset feeds multiple actions, but it competes with execution memory and can push out other blocks if overused. Cache deliberately, verify the hit in the Storage tab, and unpersist when finished.
